entities.name: Adolf of Altena
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Adolf I of Altena (c. 1157–1220) was Archbishop of Cologne from 1193 to 1205, one of the most politically turbulent archiepiscopates in that great see's history. Born into the family of the Counts of Altena — a dynasty that would give rise to the powerful Counts of the Mark and later the House of Brandenburg — Adolf was both an ecclesiastical prince and a member of a significant Westphalian noble house.

His archiepiscopate was defined by the imperial succession crisis following the death of Emperor Henry VI in 1197. Adolf initially supported Philip of Swabia for the imperial throne against Otto IV of Brunswick, but later switched his support to Otto IV — a dramatic reversal that had enormous consequences. The Archbishop of Cologne's role as a Prince-Elector gave this change of allegiance decisive weight, and Otto IV was eventually crowned emperor in 1209. Adolf's political manoeuvring during this contested succession made him one of the key figures in the Ottonian-Staufen conflict.

In 1205, Adolf was deposed from the archbishopric by Pope Innocent III — a measure of the extraordinary political turbulence of his tenure and the papacy's increasingly assertive role in resolving Church-state conflicts. His deposition exemplified Innocent III's determination to assert papal authority over the German Church at its most powerful point. Adolf's archiepiscopate is a case study in the intersection of imperial succession politics and ecclesiastical governance.
